P1.evidence: No setter code in the title and no application referenced, so the read-back check does not apply. The rep had started 22 minutes late by his own admission — 'Andrew, really wasted, yeah, to my fault, 22 minutes. So let's dive straight into it' — and set no frame at all as a result. No 'where you are, where you want to go, what's in the way, what you need', and no agreement question. Straight to the open question, which was clean: 'How can we potentially help you?' The lost frame matters here more than usual, because the frame is where 'what's in the way' gets named as a category before the prospect volunteers a spinal condition into a vacuum.

P2.evidence: The most consequential Baseline failure in the batch. Age was asked, but at 00:28:45 — after the commitment check, after the trust gauge, essentially at the point of sale — and height and weight were never obtained at all. Occupation was never asked; that he is a physician assistant emerged only because he mentioned it while describing his ministry ambitions. The clinical checks are the ones that matter and none of them ran. Scoliosis, chronic daily back symptoms, bilateral knee injuries and a completed course of physical therapy were all volunteered by the prospect inside his first answer, at 00:01:01, and the rep asked not one follow-up question about any of them: not how severe, not how long, not what the physical therapist concluded, not what his personal trainer's programme is designed to protect, and above all not who told him never to lift heavy weights or whether that advice still stands. Training week, results, diet, sleep and energy were never raised in any form. A loaded ballistic programme was designed and sold against zero collected physiological data.

P3.evidence: Excellent, and the best-run Phase 3 in this folder. The paintbrush question was properly anchored to a date that mattered to him — 'It's your wedding, right, next year. How do you really want to feel?' — and produced the strong-but-flexible answer. The bridge and the ripple sequence both ran: 'Physically, what kind of impact is that going to have in the different arenas of your life?' then 'how do you foresee that confidence being transferred into others?', which opened the girlfriend, the breakup and the masculinity thread. The rep then explicitly named the identity move and ran it: 'the final one, I guess is the most important, the identity. When you're looking at yourself, Andrew, forget the six pack and the muscles. What do you want to see in your own eyes this time next year?' The reflect-back and want-or-need were combined well — 'Andrew 2.0, the version of him that... is able to lead his girlfriend, his future kids... Would you say it's a want or a need?' — and the follow-up 'Why do you say a need?' pushed one level further into faith and identity. Only the can't-do-yet question is short of a full hit.

P4.evidence: Root cause ran well, past attempts did not. The blocker question was asked properly — 'what do you foresee actually stopping you from putting in the effort and the resources and time to actually step into the higher version of yourself?' — and the prospect named the gap himself with unusual precision: 'the only way I'm going to build discipline is where I have accountability... That's why I failed before with working out consistently, because I've never been taught how to build discipline. My dad didn't teach me that.' The rep followed the nervous-system thread and got a detailed answer. What never ran: what he has tried before as a question, what happened with any of it, and the information-isn't-the-problem challenge. The existing personal trainer of several years — an active, paid, competing solution — was never examined at all.

P5.evidence: No consequence was ever established. There is no two-year question, no cost of inaction, no settle-for and no why-not anywhere in this transcript. The rep said out loud that he was skipping ahead: 'Typically, man, I'll ask a few more questions, but I get that sense from you that now is really the time for you to act.' The one move that did run was a good one — 'when is the most appropriate time for you to step into that version, Andrew?' answered 'I mean, today', challenged with 'Are you sure? Are you sure you're not just being polite?' — which produced the most honest passage of the call about settling for less. That is a line in the sand drawn on ground that was never prepared.

P6.evidence: Correctly sequenced, which is the part the script cares about: every commitment move landed before price. The capability check was asked in almost the scripted words — 'do you personally feel internally capable of making that happen?' — 'With help. Yes. Definitely.' The trust gauge returned 9 or 10 with money named and dismissed by the prospect himself: 'the financial investment, yeah, it's a concern, but it's not going to stop me.' A clear yes existed before the offer. The all-in check is scored partial rather than hit for a specific reason: it was run at 00:19:13 as a pre-emptive block rather than a question, framing the coming decision as a fight-or-flight episode and asking in advance whether he would push through it. It obtained 'I'm all in', but it was engineered to make a later objection feel like a relapse rather than to surface one. See the flags file.

P11.evidence: Payment collection was initiated on the call — 'Okay, so I'll just get the link up for you' followed by careful confirmation of his email address — and then the recording was ended: 'What I'm going to do, obviously, sensitive information. I'll take my recorder out of this call.' The Trevor booking was described as a next step rather than executed live: 'Then I also book into a one-on-one call with Trevor.' The agreement email and the welcome-email, Skool link and questionnaire walkthrough are entirely unobservable and are marked not applicable rather than scored as failures the rep may not have committed. This is the second close in this folder where the phase disappears at exactly the same moment.

objection_plays.detail: SCRIPT GAP AND THE MOST IMPORTANT ENTRY IN THIS FILE — clinical fit. This is the documented gap from the Tyron Giuliani call, appearing here in its inverse and far more dangerous form. There, no scripted play existed and a well-funded prospect was lost. Here, no scripted play existed and the rep improvised his way through it to a $9,000 close. The trigger landed twice: 'I've always been told not to lift heavy weights... because I have scoliosis' at 00:01:01, and the direct question 'And so with scoliosis, even that shouldn't be an issue?' at 00:23:41. The improvised response was a colleague's before-and-after, an assertion that 'it's not an issue', a vague reference to x-rays, and a near-promise of 99.9% symptom removal. The correct move — pause, get it in front of the prospect's physical therapist or physician, close conditionally on clearance — does not exist anywhere in the playbook, so it was never available to be run. Building it should be the highest-priority change to the script.

The money concern was raised explicitly and tied to instability — 'I don't really know where it is monetarily... that's definitely a concern just because of this work situation I'm going through' — and not a single move of the open-wallet play ran. No isolation, no HOW-not-SHOULD frame, no permission question, and none of the six financial-picture questions. The rep's entire response was 'And I hold you accountable to that, yeah?' It surfaced a second time at the point of decision — 'it's going to be tighter financially, but I have it' — and was met with 'I don't want you to be broke. I don't want to take food off your table. But I want it to be a bit uncomfortable.' Nine thousand dollars was taken from a prospect in an unstable job whose capacity was never once established. Note the asymmetry with the Omar Maldonado call two days earlier, where the full financial-picture sequence ran on a prospect who did not buy.

Run pre-emptively rather than in response, which is what makes it worth recording separately. At 00:19:13, before any offer or price existed, the rep constructed the fear frame around the prospect's just-disclosed condition: 'when it's really time for us to help you step into that version of you, that in itself is a fight or flight moment... are you going to listen to that voice... I'm going to push forward in spite of that feeling, or are you going to choose to continue the patterns that's not really served you well till now?' That is recognisably the spirit of Objection E — the bridge, the push-through-the-feeling move — but deployed as an inoculation rather than a rebuttal, and built from material the prospect had given him about an anxiety disorder. It worked: 'I'm all in.' Scored partial on execution and flagged on conduct.

notes: Phase 3 here is the best discovery in the batch and should be clipped — the identity question and the wedding-day anchor are exemplary. Everything protective was skipped. Baseline did not run at all on the one prospect in this folder who disclosed a spinal condition, bilateral knee rehab and a standing instruction not to lift, and the Consequence Frame was announced as unnecessary. The single most actionable coaching point is not a technique: when a prospect volunteers a diagnosed structural condition in the first two minutes, the call must stop and route to a clearance question, and the playbook must give the rep a way to close conditionally on it. Second point: the open-wallet play ran fully on the prospect who did not buy and not at all on the prospect who spent $9,000 while disclosing job instability. That inversion is the pattern to correct.
